stories.headline: F1 2027 driver lineups: Who has a seat - and who's out of contract?
stories.summary: The 2026 rule changes threw Formula 1 into a new era of challenges and uncertainty, but the real moments of unpredictability are still to come.
stories.body:
The 2026 rule changes threw Formula 1 into a new era of challenges and uncertainty, but the real moments of unpredictability are still to come.

Most drivers secured short-term deals to survive the regulation shift, leaving the grid wide open for the following year. With only a handful of drivers locked into long-term contracts almost every seat on the grid is up for grabs.

Here is our early look at what the future holds for the current Formula 1 lineup.

McLaren

Lando Norris - 'multi-year deal' beyond 2030

Prior to the start of the 2024 F1 season Norris agreed to an "extended multi-year contract beyond 2025."

The reigning champion has now signed a new contract with McLaren until at least 2030. The deal, which includes one of his title-winning Formula 1 cars as a gift from the team, also has the option of a "multi-year" extension beyond 2030.

Oscar Piastri - 'multi-year deal' beyond 2026

Ahead of the first race of the 2025 F1 season Piastri also signed a multi-year contract extension. His previous deal already ran until the end of 2026, and his latest agreement is likely to keep him at McLaren until at least the end of 2028 -- though speculation continues to rumble on about his long-term future.

Ferrari

Lewis Hamilton - 2027

While an exact end date of Hamilton's contract -- signed after completing one of the biggest driver moves in F1 history -- was never officially communicated, Hamilton admitted earlier this year that he still had a contract in place for 2027. That means he got at least a three-year deal at Ferrari, something he had also been seeking at Mercedes.

Amid retirement rumours, Hamilton has also crushed speculation and assured fans that he wasn't going anywhere just yet.

He said: "There's a lot of people that are trying to retire me, and that's not even in my thoughts. I'm already thinking of what will be next, and planning for, like, the next five years. But I still plan to be here for some time."

Charles Leclerc - 2028

Leclerc, who first joined Ferrari in 2019, signed another multi-year extension ahead of the 2026 Monaco Grand Prix.

The team did not publicly reveal an exact expiry date, but the new agreement is understood to take Leclerc to 2028 and potentially beyond, giving Ferrari long-term security over one side of its driver lineup.

Red Bull

Max Verstappen - 2030

Red Bull confirmed in 2022 that four-time world champion Verstappen would remain with the team until the end of 2028 in one of the longest deals on the F1 grid.

Sources told ESPN that performance-related clauses in Verstappen's contract could allow him to leave early, but the Dutchman has now signed a new contract extension with Red Bull until 2030 ahead of the Dutch Grand Prix.

Isack Hadjar - 2027

Isack Hadjar was promoted from Racing Bulls to partner Verstappen for the 2026 season after an impressive rookie campaign. He has now signed a contract extension with Red Bull, securing his seat for the 2027 season.

Mercedes

George Russell - beyond 2026

Russell agreed a new deal with Mercedes ahead of the 2026 season following lengthy negotiations with team principal Toto Wolff.

Although the agreement was initially confirmed as taking him through at least 2026, Russell has since described it as a multi-year deal and said he will fulfill the performance clauses in his contract to stay at Mercedes next year.

Kimi Antonelli - TBC

Mercedes' Antonelli has only been given one-year contracts since his debut, but given his form this season there's no way he'll be leaving the Silver Arrows. Right?

No official announcements have been made yet, but Antonelli could be celebrating both a maiden title and a bumper new deal this year.

Aston Martin

Fernando Alonso - 2027

Alonso's current Aston Martin deal ran until the end of the 2026 season, but the 45-year-old has now confirmed his decision to keep racing with the team through 2027.

Lance Stroll - 2027

Stroll signed a contract extension in 2024 which kept him with Aston Martin for 2025 "and beyond," but no specific end date was announced. Part of that ambiguity, of course, is because he's the son of team owner Lawrence Stroll.

He remains with the team for 2026 and will continue to partner alongside Alonso for 2027.

Alpine

Pierre Gasly - 2028

Gasly is one of the drivers whose future is already settled -- the Frenchman signed a new multi-year agreement with Alpine in 2025 which keeps him locked in at the team until at least the end of the 2028 season.

Franco Colapinto - 2027

Colapinto retained his Alpine seat alongside Gasly for 2026 after taking over from Jack Doohan during the previous season. He has now signed a new contract with the team, meaning the Argentinian will continue with Alpine for the 2027 season.

Haas

Rafael Câmara - 'multi-year deal' beyond 2027

F2 star Câmara will replace Esteban Ocon for the 2027 season on a multi-year agreement. The reigning Formula 3 champion and current Formula 2 leader will make his debut in F1 and will partner fellow Ferrari Driver Academy member Oliver Bearman.

Oliver Bearman - TBC

Bearman joined Haas on a multi-year deal when he became a full-time F1 driver in 2025. The exact duration of Bearman's contract has not been made public, leaving his 2027 status uncertain for now.

However, sources with good knowledge of the team's thinking have told ESPN that Bearman is almost certain to stay with the team in 2027 unless a Ferrari seat opens up, then the Englishman remains effectively loaned to Haas.

Racing Bulls

Liam Lawson - 2027

Lawson remained with Racing Bulls for 2026 after rebuilding his season following a short-lived promotion to Red Bull the previous year.

His seat was only confirmed for the current season, but the New Zealander has proved his case after a series of strong performances, meaning he has now secured his seat for the 2027 season.

Arvid Lindblad - 2027

Lindblad became the latest Red Bull junior to make the jump to Formula 1 when he was handed a Racing Bulls seat for 2026.

The rookie was only confirmed for this season, but will now partner alongside Lawson for 2027.

Williams

Carlos Sainz - 'multi-year deal' beyond 2026

Sainz originally joined Williams on a deal covering the 2025 and 2026 seasons, with "options to extend" his stay beyond that. He has recently spoken about wanting to make the Williams project work, leading to him signing a new multi-year extension with the team.

Alex Albon - 2027

Albon signed a new one-year contract with Williams during the summer break, tying him down for the 2027 season. The short-term deal is interesting, given Albon's last contract -- signed in 2024 -- was for multiple years. Keeping those options open?

Audi

Nico Hulkenberg - TBC

Hulkenberg joined Sauber ahead of its transformation into the Audi team on a multi-year contract in 2025.

There are believed to be options in his deal which could allow him to remain with Audi beyond 2026, but an exact end date has not been announced.

Gabriel Bortoleto - TBC

Bortoleto joined Hulkenberg at Sauber before the team's transition to Audi and also signed a multi-year deal.

The Brazilian is contracted through at least the end of 2026, but his place for 2027 has not yet been officially confirmed.

Cadillac

Sergio Perez - 2029

Perez returned to the Formula 1 grid with newcomers Cadillac for the team's debut season in 2026 after spending a year away from racing.

The Mexican joined on a multi-year agreement and has now extended his contract which will see him stay with the American team until 2029.

Valtteri Bottas - 2027

Valtteri Bottas also returned to a full-time race seat with Cadillac after spending 2025 as Mercedes' reserve driver.

The Finn signed a multi-year deal which runs until at least the end of 2027, giving the new team one of the few already settled driver pairings heading into next season.

stories.headline: Manchester United finally get Mauricio Pochettino after a decade of near misses
stories.summary: After years of near misses and missed opportunities, Mauricio Pochettino is finally taking charge at Manchester United following a decade-long pursuit.
stories.body:
It feels a bit like destiny for Mauricio Pochettino to end up at Manchester United. After all, their flirtation with the former Tottenham Hotspur, Paris Saint-Germain and U.S. men's national team manager began more than 10 years ago.

In May 2016, amid mounting doubts over Louis van Gaal's future, Sir Alex Ferguson asked to meet Pochettino at a London restaurant. Jose Mourinho was already being lined up to replace Van Gaal, but Ferguson still asked the League Managers Association secretary for Pochettino's number.

The two-hour lunch at Scott's Restaurant in Mayfair would have stayed private, except the pair -- and Pochettino's assistant Jesus Perez -- were caught by paparazzi on the street outside.

Concerned about the speculation, Tottenham insisted it was just a "social occasion between colleagues." To quiet the noise further, they moved up an announcement that Pochettino had verbally agreed to a new five-year contract. Mourinho was confirmed as Van Gaal's successor weeks later.

United have made five permanent appointments since Pochettino's meeting with Ferguson and the former Argentina defender has never been far away.

When Mourinho was sacked in December 2018, Pochettino -- impressing at Spurs -- was considered the top choice for many Old Trafford executives. But with Pochettino under contract at Tottenham, Ole Gunnar Solskjaer was given the caretaker role to steady the ship. Solskjaer won his first five games and in January 2019, United traveled to Spurs and won 1-0 to make it six from six.

Sources at United said there was no "defining moment" that decided Solskjaer would get the job permanently, but victory over Pochettino's Spurs was viewed as "a very positive sign." Two months later, Solskjaer signed a three-year deal; Pochettino was sacked by Tottenham in November 2019, five months after reaching the UEFA Champions League final.

Out of work and available, his name hung over Solskjaer's reign every time there was a blip. It reached the point in January 2021 that United bosses admitted they were "relieved" when Pochettino took over at Paris Saint-Germain. The feeling at the time was that the speculation had become a distraction and that Solskjaer would get more breathing space with Pochettino out of the picture as a potential replacement.

Solskjaer lasted another 11 months. When the Norwegian was sacked in November 2021, United opted for another caretaker in Ralf Rangnick and Pochettino was earmarked early on as a potential permanent appointment at the end of the season. It never materialized.

Form under Rangnick at the end of the 2021-22 season was so bad that United wanted to lift the mood and announce a permanent successor before the end of the campaign. In the end, it was a close call between Pochettino and Erik ten Hag. Crucially, Ajax allowed Ten Hag to negotiate with United during the season. Locked in a battle for the Ligue 1 title, PSG barred Pochettino from doing the same. It was one of the reasons Ten Hag won the job and his appointment was announced in April 2022. Pochettino left PSG two months later.

With Ten Hag's job hanging by a thread after the 2023-24 season, Pochettino was interviewed again. He met the hierarchy shortly after leaving Chelsea in May 2024, but United bosses went away thinking that he had been burned by his time at PSG and Stamford Bridge.

Omar Berrada and Jason Wilcox -- part of the delegation that met Pochettino -- liked him, but felt it wasn't the right moment and eventually stuck with Ten Hag. By the time the Dutchman was finally sacked in October 2024, Pochettino was already in place as head coach of the United States national team -- two months into a two-year contract ahead of a home FIFA World Cup.

Pochettino's credentials were reviewed again towards the end of last season when Sir Jim Ratcliffe, Berrada and Wilcox were weighing up whether or not to appoint Michael Carrick permanently.

Managers at the World Cup --- Pochettino, Thomas Tuchel and Julian Nagelsmann -- were initially considered before being ruled over a matter of timing.

Carrick signed a two-year contract in May. Pochettino was still involved at the World Cup until early July -- when the U.S. lost to Belgium in the round of 16 -- just weeks before United's preseason schedule was due to begin.

With Carrick sacked just 15 games into his permanent tenure, it's finally Pochettino's turn.

There's admiration internally for highly-rated young coaches like Kieran McKenna and Fabian Hürzeler, but there's a feeling that it's not the right time to hire a relatively inexperienced up-and-coming manager.

Pochettino ticks the boxes for Premier League experience after spells at Southampton, Tottenham and Chelsea and big club experience with PSG. He also has history with big players like Lionel Messi, Neymar and Kylian Mbappé.

Berrada and Wilcox have found him to be re-energized compared to their meeting in 2024, and he's already spoken about his ambition to win the Premier League and the Champions League.

Pochettino did his bit to get the move over the line by asking representatives to inform United of the existence of a release clause in the contract extension he signed with the U.S. in August. United feel it's the right time to appoint Pochettino, who they consider both tactically astute and a good leader who can handle the glare of the Old Trafford spotlight.

For almost half of his 17-year career in the dugout, Pochettino has been pursued by United only for the stars to never quite align. A decade on from his lunch with Ferguson, he will finally get the chance to fill his shoes.

stories.headline: Ravens' Humphrey apologizes for quip that Baltimore 'best at making criminals'
stories.summary: Ravens cornerback Marlon Humphrey apologized Wednesday for the derogatory comment he recently made about Baltimore on his podcast.
stories.body:
OWINGS MILLS, Md. -- Outspoken Ravens cornerback Marlon Humphrey apologized for the derogatory comment he made about the city of Baltimore on his recent podcast.

On an episode of "The Marlon Humphrey Show" released Wednesday, Humphrey took a swipe at the city when asked what Baltimore was best at making.

After first mentioning "The Star-Spangled Banner" and National Bohemian beer, Humphrey quipped, "They're best at making criminals."

After Wednesday's practice, Humphrey said he regretted those remarks.

"I would like to apologize for some comments on my podcast I had to the city of Baltimore," Humphrey said. "As you guys know, I've been here my whole career. Spent lots of offseasons here. Welcomed a son here and I'm an investor in the city. And obviously, I do know the effect that words have and just like to apologize for those comments."

Humphrey received heavy fan backlash on social media Wednesday afternoon. The podcast episode featuring Humphrey's "criminals" comment has since been deleted from his YouTube page.

Baltimore Mayor Brandon Scott acknowledged Humphrey's apology in a statement posted to social media, but noted, "a verbal apology is not enough. Baltimore is a city full of young Black boys who look to the Ravens as a beacon of light in their lives and to have someone that looks like them who wears a Baltimore Ravens jersey relegate them to becoming criminals cuts deeper.

"I wonder how he would feel if prominent Baltimoreans used their platforms to imply that Baltimore once produced great defensive backs but we have recently lost our way."

Scott then added, "They wouldn't do that because our team and city are supposed to be united as one. Baltimore versus the world."

Scott concluded his post by inviting Humphrey to sit down with him and some Baltimore citizens "who have re-entered into our community and are now preventing others from making the mistakes they made."

Humphrey, 30, is in his 10th season with Baltimore and is the longest-tenured defensive player on the Ravens. The No. 16 selection in the 2017 draft by Baltimore, Humphrey has been to four Pro Bowls, which are the most by a Ravens cornerback.

In recent years, Humphrey has struggled and has drawn the ire of fans. This season, he has given up an NFL-worst 313 yards in coverage in the fourth quarter.

Asked if he understood why fans would be upset with this comment even if he was joking, Humphrey replied, "Yeah, I just apologized ... and that won't really happen again."

Humphrey is in the final year of a five-year, $97.5 million extension. His $26.276 million salary cap hit is the largest for any cornerback in 2026.

Humphrey's slight at Baltimore comes at a time when the franchise is dealing with one of its worst stretches in its history. The Ravens (4-6) have lost five straight, including a 23-20 loss to the previously winless Los Angeles Chargers on Monday. Baltimore has also lost seven of its past eight games at home.

Ravens coach Jesse Minter said he would keep any conversations with Humphrey about this matter private.

"Just speaking for myself, I love this city," Minter said. "I know what this city means to me and my family. I take a lot of pride in being here. It's a great city with a bunch of great people. We desperately want to represent this city the right way by how we play most importantly."

This isn't the first time that Humphrey has caused a stir with his podcast. One month ago, Humphrey said safety Kyle Hamilton "knew" he was going to make a game-sealing interception of Atlanta Falcons quarterback Tua Tagovailoa once he replaced injured starter Michael Penix Jr. in overtime. Hamilton later shot down that characterization, describing Humphrey's account as "pretty hyperbolic."

"I think Marlon is very unapologetically himself," Hamilton said Wednesday. "He can be slightly abrasive at times, but that's just him. And talking to his family has always been like that. But we all love Marlon and we appreciate everything he's done for us [and] will do for us. And he's one of us."

Humphrey has been a target of fan criticism over the past two seasons. He has been frequently booed during home games at M&T Bank Stadium.

During the "Monday Night Football" broadcast two days ago, when the Ravens were losing to the winless Chargers, fans could be heard shouting "F--- Marlon Humphrey" as they exited the stadium.

"I love the city. I think I've expressed this many times," Humphrey said. "I want to win in front of the fans just because it's not cheap to be in those seats."

Has the fans' negativity toward him affected his view of them?

"To answer your question," Humphrey replied, "nothing has changed how I feel."

stories.headline: 2026-27 MLB free agency, trade grades: Offseason analysis
stories.summary: We've got you covered with grades and analysis on every winter signing and big offseason trade.
stories.body:
Hot stove season has finally begun!

The 2026-27 MLB offseason is officially here, and we have you covered with grades and analysis for every major signing and trade as this winter -- which is expected to include a labor stoppage -- unfolds.

Whether it's a franchise-changing free agent signing or an unexpected blockbuster trade, we'll weigh in with what it all means for next season and beyond.

ESPN MLB experts Bradford Doolittle and David Schoenfield will evaluate each move as it happens, so follow along here, as this story will continue to be updated. Check back in for all the most recent analysis.

Related links: Tracker | Top 50 free agents

Twins bring Gray back to Minnesota
The deal: Two years, $55 million

Grade: B+

Sonny Gray had one of the best seasons of his career with the Minnesota Twins back in 2023, when he made 32 starts, posted a 2.79 ERA and a 5.6 WAR, and finished second in the Cy Young Award voting. (He won just eight games, plagued by a lack of run support and a poor bullpen.) The Twins are hoping for a happy reunion, signing Gray to the largest total value free agent pitcher contract in franchise history (tied with a four-year deal for Ervin Santana back in 2015). The second year is a player option, so this could end up being a one-year deal.

This wasn't necessarily where everyone expected Gray to land, especially coming off a strong season with the Boston Red Sox. He finished 18-5, tied with Cristopher Sanchez for the major league lead in wins, while posting a 2.72 ERA, good for eighth in the majors. While Gray had some injuries earlier in his career, he has been durable across the past four seasons, averaging 30 starts and 175 innings. That almost makes him Old Hoss Radbourn in today's game. While Gray's ERA has jumped all over the place, his FIP (fielding independent pitching) speaks to more consistency, with marks of 3.40, 2.83, 3.12, 3.39 and 3.47 going back to 2022.

The negatives: Gray is 37 years old and his strikeout rate took a big dip in 2026, dropping from 28.4% over the previous two seasons to 21.8%. That's still playable -- the MLB average for starting pitchers was 21.9% -- but it's something to watch. However, he's such a smart pitcher -- mixing in six different pitches with excellent command -- that he can succeed even with a lower K rate.

It's a nice move for the Twins, who ranked 22nd in rotation ERA this past season. They've indicated an intent to keep Joe Ryan. Plus, Pablo Lopez is aiming to be ready by Opening Day in his return from Tommy John surgery, so Minnesota could roll out a rotation of Gray, Ryan, Lopez, Taj Bradley (their top starter in 2026 with 4.4 WAR) and Bailey Ober, with Dean Kremer, Connor Prielipp and Zebby Matthews as depth. Ryan, Lopez, Ober and Kremer are all in the final years of their deals, so there are trade possibilities here, especially since Minnesota needs to improve the bullpen.

Gray's contract projection was for two years and $42 million, so the deal comes in higher than that; this might be par for the course for starting pitchers given Dustin May's inflated three-year, $52.5 million deal with the Chicago White Sox. In one sense, the best-case scenario for the Twins is if Gray has another good season and he opts out. If he does have a good season and Lopez bounces back, this has a chance to be a really nice rotation, with Prielipp having breakout potential in his second year. And a good rotation in the American League Central will make the Twins contenders. -- Schoenfield

Mariners add Garcia to infield in six-player swap

Seattle Mariners get:

IF Maikel Garcia

RHP James McArthur

RHP L.P. Langevin

Kansas City Royals get:

RHP Bryce Miller

RHP Logan Evans

LHP Jose Ferrer

Mariners grade: A-

Garcia is the best player in the deal, and the difference is enough to make this a slam dunk win for Seattle. Nagging injuries undermined Garcia's 2026 season after his breakout the year before; but even so, his contract and patience at the plate remained well above average, and he was still one of baseball's top defensive third basemen. While the injuries cost him in the power department and on the bases, Garcia is entering his age-27 season as a good bet to bounce back to All-Star form. His well-documented penchant for self-improvement also supports the argument for positive regression.

Under contract through 2031 on team-friendly terms, Garcia is a major upgrade at a soft spot on the Mariners' depth chart. Seattle's defensive projection at the hot corner leaped from 21st to first in my system, and the offensive leap in runs from that spot was about 10 spots, to No. 12. Garcia's range will only help the overall infield defense, as he will team with Colt Emerson, Cole Young and Josh Naylor to give Seattle a pretty dynamic group.

The Mariners had the kind of surplus on their organizational rotation chart to easily absorb the loss of Miller. Similar to last year, they look a little thin in bullpen lefties, but Ferrer didn't prove to be the splash addition in that role Seattle hoped for anyway. McArthur is a sneaky get here. He hasn't pitched in the majors since 2024 because of injury but was closing games for the Royals before getting hurt. He's a worthy flier. Langevin is a lower-level prospect, a righty with big strikeout rates and shaky command.

The Mariners' right-now win projection climbs over 90 with this trade, and at 67% division title odds, Seattle is a heavy early favorite in a soft division. This trade only bolsters the chances that the Mariners bounce back in 2027 to become the team we thought they were in 2026.

Royals grade: C-

The Royals just don't have the kind of organizational depth to be trading one of their few difference-makers for a package of pitchers who in total upgrade their staff only marginally and offer little collective upside. In the near term, the trade makes the Royals worse, and the problems only compound from here given that they had Garcia under team control for so long.

Miller moves right into a middle-of-the-rotation slot for the Royals, and if Michael Wacha declines, it's possible Miller will be Kansas City's top starter next season. Still, Miller, 27, has a career ERA+ of 95 and is at 80 over the past two seasons, both of which have been undermined by injury. For the Royals, the hope would be that Miller is ready to take the kind of leap that Wacha and Seth Lugo did when they joined the Royals. And to be fair, Miller's Statcast metrics definitely suggest that could happen.

Ferrer, as mentioned, had a poor season in Seattle after being acquired for catcher Harry Ford. Ferrer has a career OPS+ of 96 but still becomes the Royals' top bullpen lefty, almost by default. Evans was a ranked organizational prospect in Seattle and had a decent debut season in 2025. He underwent Tommy John surgery, the internal brace version, in January. He projected with mid- to lower-rotation upside before getting hurt.

The instant change in the Royals' projection kind of tells the story. The new pitchers are pushing not-great pitchers down the depth chart, so Kansas City's profile improves by about 16 runs on the prevention side. Garcia's defensive loss is fairly marginal for Kansas City, as Nick Loftin is a good defender, as well. But the loss of the bat is about a 17-run hit for the Royals' run production.

The end result? The same amount of bad, just shaped differently. The Royals should have received more for a player of Garcia's ability and contract. -- Doolittle

White Sox add midrotation piece with May
The deal: Three years, $52.5 million

Grade: D+

We've had two significant signings off the free agent market so far, and both involve freshly minted ex-Milwaukee Brewers: After Jake Bauers landed with the Boston Red Sox on Friday, the Chicago White Sox plucked Dustin May off the championship Milwaukee pitching staff.

Whereas Boston was banking on Bauers' 2026 breakout being his current true talent level, the White Sox are perhaps taking a bigger gamble that May's past five years do not represent his real level of ability. Since his early shine as a top Los Angeles Dodgers prospect, which included some promising early work in the majors, May's career has been journeyman-like. Around injuries that cost him the 2024 season, he has put up 0.9 bWAR with a 91 ERA+ over 356 big-league innings for the period covering 2022 through last season.

May became a fallback addition for the Brewers at the 2026 trade deadline after more glitzy pursuits (ahem, Tarik Skubal) fell short. May put up a 106 ERA+ for the St. Louis Cardinals before the trade and, given the Brewers' track record with acquired pitchers, you had to figure the move boded well for an even better post-trade performance. But that's not what happened. May had a 5.65 ERA and 75 ERA+ over 10 starts for the Brewers and was not a core part of Milwaukee's postseason rotation.

This uninspiring platform performance partially explains the grade above, but only partially. We'll see how things shake out in the market when we have more signings to work from -- May is the first pitcher to land a sizable deal -- but this seems like an overpay at least in terms of years. ESPN's Kiley McDaniel projected a one-year, $14 million deal for May, while a consensus projection from various outlets looked something more like two years, $24.7 million.

The White Sox are likely banking on May's tantalizing tracking data, which in 2026 had him in the 85th percentile in fastball velocity (average of 96.8 mph) and 72nd percentile in extension. Indeed, my own projection model sees enough in May keeping his value that it suggested a three-year, $45.9 million deal would be justified, which at least is in the neighborhood of what he got from the White Sox.

As it stands, May slots in behind Grant Taylor in the revamped Chicago rotation, just ahead of Sean Burke and Luis Castillo. Ah, Castillo: Is he a cautionary tale for a White Sox approach that liked him, as it likes May, despite underwhelming results before the deal? We'll see. May is also pushing pitchers such as David Sandlin and Davis Martin down in the pecking order, though there's no guarantee he's going to be that much better than them, if at all. I've got May adding 0.9 wins to Chicago's right-now roster, which pushes its 2027 playoff odds up by about three percentage points.

That's fairly marginal when you remember that the White Sox were overachievers in 2026. It was a great story, but it also means their starting baseline is somewhere south of the 84 games they won in 2026. If they are really looking to bolster their chances heading into 2027 -- and beyond -- then opportunity cost comes into play even though the White Sox should have some remaining spending capacity, or at least you would hope so. Would a little patience have netted them someone like Sonny Gray, Michael King or Freddy Peralta?

If the White Sox still go after someone like that and the May signing doesn't end up as their one big rotation splash, then maybe we push that grade up to the C-minus range. Given what we know at the moment, though, I'm underwhelmed. -- Doolittle

Red Sox get offensive boost with Bauers addition

The deal: Four years, $58 million

Grade: A

The Red Sox weren't high on anybody's list of teams likely to sign Jake Bauers given they already have an All-Star first baseman in Willson Contreras, but this signing is an early candidate for best move of the offseason. The grade reflects two thoughts: (1) that Bauers' breakout -- he finished 11th in the majors in OPS and third in on-base percentage this past season -- is for real; and (2) that the contract is a steal at $14.5 million per year.

Bauers will be entering his age-31 season, and, of course, spent years struggling in the majors before finally figuring things out, so while there would generally be concern that his 2026 season was a fluke, all the advanced metrics suggest the opposite. His Statcast numbers: 93rd percentile bat speed, 94th percentile hard-hit rate, 93rd percentile chase rate, 98th percentile walk rate. Those are real skills that aren't going to diminish overnight and should allow him to remain a productive hitter (he even hit left-handers well, so should project as a full-time player). Everyone saw the quality of his at-bats during the postseason throughout the Milwaukee Brewers' title run; he was named MVP of the National League Championship Series.

As for the contract, compare it to Josh Naylor's deal last year, when he signed a five-year, $92.5 million contract with the Seattle Mariners. Naylor was two years younger, but he was coming off a 129-OPS+, 3.0-WAR season compared with Bauers' 140 OPS+ and 3.3 WAR. Yes, Naylor had the longer track record of success but less power and a lower OBP. Signing Bauers for $58 million looks like a potential bargain.

Contreras is under contract for 2027 with a team option for 2028 and is the better fielder, so Bauers slots in as the DH. That leaves Roman Anthony, Ceddanne Rafaela and Wilyer Abreu in the outfield. Masataka Yoshida is still around for one more year as a backup, and the Red Sox will likely look to trade Jarren Duran, who still has two years of team control but is estimated to make $11.1 million in arbitration. With Duran coming off a bad season at the plate, the Red Sox might non-tender him if they can't trade him.

No doubt there will be criticism that the Red Sox needed a right-handed batter instead, but they actually had a slightly higher OPS against left-handers (.734 to .710). They just needed a good hitter, regardless of which side of the plate he stands on.

Remember that they also acquired the right-handed Curtis Mead from the Washington Nationals only to see him get injured in his first game with them. He'll be back and should slot in at second base. Boston also has shortstop Franklin Arias, one of the top three or four prospects in the minors who demolished Double- and Triple-A this year. Indeed, if Bauers comes close to his 2026 numbers and Anthony hits like everyone thought he was going to in 2026, this could be one of the best lineups in the league:

LF Anthony (L)

RF Abreu (L)

1B Contreras (R)

DH Bauers (L)

CF Rafaela (R)

2B Mead (R)

C Adley Rutschman (S)

SS Arias (R) / Trevor Story (R)

3B Caleb Durbin (R)

As for the Brewers, it's sad to see a postseason hero go, although not necessarily unexpected. They could have afforded this contract, but they have first-base prospects just about ready in Andrew Fischer, who led the minors with 48 home runs, and Blake Burke, who hit 34 home runs and stole 29 bases. They also have Andrew Vaughn on hand as a placeholder if Fischer and Burke aren't ready. Plus, they might need this money to sign William Contreras to a long-term extension. The Brewers will be fine. -- Schoenfield

Braves bolster bullpen by landing Phillips
The deal: Three years, $35 million

Grade: B-

The Atlanta Braves don't go after the biggest free agents -- B.J. Upton's $75 million deal in 2013 remains the largest free agent contract in franchise history -- but president of baseball operations Alex Anthopoulos does like to strike as early as possible in the offseason, and he did that again with Evan Phillips.

Phillips will essentially take the roster spot of Raisel Iglesias, so the Braves will get a little younger and maybe a little better, although Iglesias had a good season as the closer in 2026 following some bumps in 2025. The Braves had one of the best bullpens in the majors this past year, leading in win probability added while ranking fourth in ERA and sixth in OPS allowed. Iglesias departs as a free agent, but Didier Fuentes or Robert Suarez can replace him as the ninth-inning guy, with Phillips likely slotting in as a setup man alongside lefties Dylan Lee and Dylan Dodd.

Phillips was one of the best relievers in the majors with the Dodgers in 2022-23 before suffering shoulder and elbow injuries at the end of the 2024 season and finally undergoing Tommy John surgery in June 2025. He returned to make 31 appearances with the Dodgers in 2026, finishing with 33 strikeouts and just six walks in 26 innings. The stuff looked good -- he was throwing a little harder than pre-injury -- although he did serve up five home runs, and his injury history makes a three-year deal a little risky.

The belief was that the Braves' pitching priority this offseason would be a starter, but signing Phillips will allow them to stretch out Fuentes as a starter in spring training. He does have a three-pitch arsenal in his fastball, slider and splitter, and he has thrown a curveball in the past, so as effective as Fuentes was in relief as a rookie in 2026, it makes sense to see if it can work out for him in the rotation. -- Schoenfield

Tigers kick off free agency with Pagan deal

The deal: One year, $11.5 million

Grade: C

A key reason the Detroit Tigers finished 76-86 despite a plus-71 run differential was the bullpen: Despite finishing 12th in ERA, it ranked 26th in win probability added, so it performed worse in high-leverage situations. Out with Kenley Jansen, in with Emilio Pagan, who has been the Reds' closer the past two seasons.

Jansen was only 22-for-28 in saves in 2026, so maybe Pagan is only a small upgrade, but like Jansen, Pagan has been prone to the home run, serving up 17 in 111⅓ innings over the past two seasons. The Tigers are betting that getting out of Cincinnati -- where he allowed 12 of those 17 home runs -- will help. Pagan is a three-pitch reliever, with a splitter that he throws primarily to left-handers and a cutter he throws to right-handers. But his 95 mph fastball is rather pedestrian for a modern closer, and batters have hit 12 home runs off it the past two seasons.

Pagan is also turning 36 years old and his fastball velo dropped from 95.8 mph in 2025 to 94.9 in 2026, so there are a couple of red flags here. The Tigers had to add somebody to the bullpen, and doing so before the anticipated lockout is logical, but Pagan projects as a midtier closer rather than the elite guy Detroit needs. Kyle Finnegan and Will Vest both struggled in 2026, so the Tigers could still nab a reliable right-handed setup guy. -- Schoenfield

stories.headline: Kayla Harrison, Amanda Nunes reclaim leading roles in women's P4P top 10
stories.summary: Who do Kayla Harrison and Amanda Nunes replace in ESPN's P4P women's top 10?
stories.body:
Hello (again), Kayla Harrison and Amanda Nunes. Goodbye (for now), Valentina Shevchenko and Zhang Weili. The top of the ESPN women's MMA pound-for-pound rankings has a new look.

Harrison and Nunes, both of whom had been ineligible for the top 10 because of inactivity, returned over the weekend for a clash of elites at UFC 334. Harrison, defending her bantamweight championship for the first time after nearly a year and a half out of the cage while healing from surgery for herniated discs in her neck, scored a fourth-round submission of Nunes, who had been retired for nearly 3½ years. As a result, Harrison takes over the No. 1 ranking and Nunes, a former two-division champion and the consensus GOAT of women's MMA, is No. 2.

The former occupants of those spots, Shevchenko and Zhang, are newly ineligible for the rankings because it's been over a year since they have fought and they have nothing scheduled. Those two former champions drop out, and the rest of the women's top 10 remains the same.

In the men's rankings, UFC heavyweight champion Ciryl Gane moves up one spot to No. 7 on the strength of his decision win over Josh Hokit in their title bout at UFC 334.

For the ESPN divisional MMA rankings, click here.

Note: Results are current; rankings are as of Nov. 18. To be eligible for the rankings, a fighter must have competed over the past 12 months or must have an upcoming fight booked. Fighters who have been dropped for inactivity can be reinstated only after they compete.

Women's pound-for-pound rankings

1. Kayla Harrison

UFC bantamweight champion

Previous ranking: Unranked

Record: 20-1

Last: W (Sub4) vs. Amanda Nunes, Nov. 14

Next: TBA

Harrison stepped into the Octagon at UFC 334 already a reigning champion, but her submission win over Nunes was truly her crowning achievement. The backstory about their shared training gym history added drama to the buildup, but what mattered most about this matchup was that Harrison, who had voiced her goal to be the greatest ever in women's MMA, was facing the woman who has lived up to that standard. After choking out Nunes, what can Harrison do for an encore? Can any other woman in the sport give her a fight? Maybe it won't come to that. Harrison and Nunes both called for a rematch -- but at featherweight. That would lessen Harrison's burden in dealing with her toughest foe: the weigh-in scale.

2. Amanda Nunes

UFC bantamweight

Previous ranking: Unranked

Record: 23-6

Last: L (Sub4) vs. Kayla Harrison, Nov. 14

Next: TBA

Nunes' return from retirement did not go as she had hoped, but her failing was not so much about deteriorated physical abilities as it was about her ill-advised choice to venture too much into the grappling wheelhouse of Harrison, a two-time Olympic judo gold medalist. If Nunes gets the rematch both women are calling for, but this time at 145 pounds, that would seem to be to the advantage of Harrison, the bigger woman. But a redo would give Nunes another opportunity to lean into her own prodigious strength as a striker.

3. Cris Cyborg

PFL featherweight champion

Record: 30-2, 1 NC

Last: W (UD) vs. Ketlen Vieira, Aug. 22

Next: TBA

It had been a while since Cyborg had fought an elite opponent in MMA until she met Larissa Pacheco in 2024. That was a legitimate matchup -- and many within the industry were predicting Cyborg's downfall. Instead, she took out the PFL's two-weight champion, upending all of Pacheco's momentum. One of the original pioneers of women's MMA is once again a champion after getting her second career submission at PFL Lyon in December. The PFL promoted her fight with Vieira as a retirement bout, but after her win Cyborg did not sound like someone who is done fighting.

4. Natalia Silva

UFC flyweight champion

Record: 21-5-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Wang Cong, Oct. 3

Next: TBA

Silva was looking every bit the part of a future UFC champion following a dominant display against Alexa Grasso at UFC 315 and a victory over Rose Namajunas at UFC 324. And now she has fulfilled that expectation, beating Wang at UFC 332 to win the belt vacated by injured Valentina Shevchenko. Silva's stick-and-move style has frustrated even the highest level of opponent, and she's got youth on her side as she won't turn 30 until 2027.

5. Mackenzie Dern

UFC strawweight champion

Record: 17-5

Last: W (UD) vs. Gillian Robertson, Aug. 15

Next: TBA

Dern's rise to the 115-pound throne was truly a changing of the guard. She is the division's first first-time champion since 2019, because the previous three champs -- Zhang Weili, Carla Esparza and Rose Namajunas -- all were in their second reigns. Dern, nearly a decade into her MMA career after multiple jiu-jitsu world championships, has won four fights in a row, including a dominant performance against a fellow grappling-heavy fighter, Robertson, in her first title defense.

6. Alexa Grasso

UFC flyweight

Record: 18-5-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Manon Fiorot, Sept. 12

Next: TBA

Grasso went nearly three years without winning a fight, but her 2023 win right before the skid was a huge one, a submission of Valentina Shevchenko for the UFC title. What followed were two more fights with Shevchenko -- a draw, then a loss -- and then a loss to Natalia Silva. But she reasserted herself with a finish of Maycee Barber in March, then got the best of Fiorot, a fellow title contender, at Noche UFC to put herself in position for another title shot.

7. Tatiana Suarez

UFC strawweight

Record: 13-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Virna Jandiroba, Nov. 7

Next: TBA

If Suarez was still feeling the effects of last year's humbling defeat to Zhang Weili in a title challenge, she certainly didn't show it at UFC 327, overcoming early adversity to thrash Loopy Godínez. Then she went on to beat another fellow top-10 strawweight, Jandiroba, sending a message to the division that Suarez is going to be a tough out for anyone at 115 pounds.

8. Dakota Ditcheva

PFL flyweight

Record: 16-0

Last: W (UD) vs. Denise Kielholtz, July 31

Next: TBA

Not only did Ditcheva win the PFL's flyweight season in 2024, but she did so in spectacular fashion -- a TKO finish over Taila Santos, who once challenged for a UFC title. Ditcheva fought only once in 2025, dominating Sumiko Inaba in the co-main event of the first PFL Champions Series card in Cape Town, South Africa. She then spent over a year on the sideline, healing injuries to both hands, before returning at PFL New York with a dominant win over Kielholtz.

9. Manon Fiorot

UFC flyweight

Record: 13-3

Last: L (UD) vs. Alexa Grasso, Sept. 12

Next: TBA

Fiorot had handled everyone the UFC put in front of her -- except the champion, Valentina Shevchenko, who defeated the Frenchwoman at UFC 315 in May 2025. But then, with another title shot within her grasp, Fiorot ran into Grasso, a former champion, at Noche UFC and lost a competitive fight.

10. Jasmine Jasudavicius

UFC flyweight

Record: 16-4

Last: W (UD) vs. Erin Blanchfield, Oct. 17

Next: TBA

Jasudavicius was rising in the 125-pound division until being knocked out by Manon Fiorot last year, halting a five-fight winning streak. But she got back up and won two in a row, most recently an impressive grappling performance against Blanchfield, to reassert herself as a contender.

Other fighter receiving votes: Joselyne Edwards and Virna Jandiroba.

How our panel voted
Brett Okamoto: 1. Kayla Harrison; 2. Amanda Nunes; 3. Mackenzie Dern; 4. Natalia Silva; 5. Tatiana Suarez; 6. Cris Cyborg; 7. Alexa Grasso; 8. Manon Fiorot; 9. Dakota Ditcheva; 10. Virna Jandiroba.

Carlos Contreras Legaspi: 1. Harrison; 2. Cyborg; 3. Silva; 4. Nunes; 5. Dern; 6. Grasso; 7. Ditcheva; 8. Suarez; 9. Fiorot; 10. Jasmine Jasudavicius.

Andrew Davis: 1. Harrison; 2. Nunes; 3. Cyborg; 4. Silva; 5. Dern; 6. Grasso; 7. Ditcheva; 8. Fiorot; 9. Suarez; 10. Jasudavicius.

Dre Waters: 1. Harrison; 2. Cyborg; 3. Nunes; 4. Dern; 5. Silva; 6. Grasso; 7. Ditcheva; 8. Suarez; 9. Fiorot; 10. Joselyne Edwards.

Jeff Wagenheim: 1. Harrison; 2. Nunes; 3. Cyborg; 4. Silva; 5. Grasso; 6. Dern; 7. Fiorot; 8. Suarez; 9. Ditcheva; 10. Jasudavicius.

Men's pound-for-pound rankings

1. Islam Makhachev

UFC welterweight champion

Record: 29-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Ian Machado Garry, Aug. 15

Next: TBA

Makhachev vacated the UFC lightweight championship to go for a second title at welterweight. By winning that belt last November with a thrashing of Jack Della Maddalena, Makhachev staked his place among MMA's greatest -- not just in today's sport but of all time. His win over Machado Garry at UFC 330 was his 17th straight, breaking the UFC record for consecutive wins. Makhachev is piling up unprecedented achievements.

2. Alexander Volkanovski

UFC featherweight champion

Record: 29-4

Last: W (TKO2) vs. Movsar Evloev, Oct. 24

Next: TBA

It felt as if the sport had started to write Volkanovski's eulogy following his knockout loss to Ilia Topuria in February 2024. Volkanovski noticed and made a point of proving to everyone he still has plenty left by recapturing the featherweight belt at UFC 314, the first of two consecutive wins over Lopes. His age (38) will likely continue to be a prefight topic, which is fine because Volkanovski enjoys proving people wrong. He did just that by handing Evloev his first loss at UFC 333.

3. Petr Yan

UFC bantamweight champion

Record: 21-5

Last: W (UD) vs. Merab Dvalishvili, Oct. 24

Next: TBA

What a return to the top it's been for Yan. He began his career with 15 consecutive wins before going on a 1-4 run from 2021 to 2023. That almost doesn't feel real now, after watching him reclaim his throne against Dvalishvili, who once handed him the worst loss of his career, then completing his trilogy with Dvalishvili with a successful title defense. Yan took a major detour, but this was the destination we felt he was capable of before the skid. He once again looks like one of the best fighters on the planet.

4. Ilia Topuria

UFC lightweight

Record: 17-1

Last: L (TKO4) vs. Justin Gaethje, June 14

Next: TBA

Topuria was an undefeated two-division champion when he ran into Gaethje at UFC Freedom 250 and was brutalized in a stoppage loss. How will that affect the immediate future of Topuria? His knockout wins over two of the greatest featherweights, Alexander Volkanovski and Max Holloway, gave him an intimidating aura. Can the former champion get that back?

5. Justin Gaethje

UFC lightweight champion

Record: 28-5

Last: W (TKO4) vs. Ilia Topuria, June 14

Next: TBA

Gaethje has spent his 15-year career thrilling MMA fans, but before the title bout on the White House lawn, all he had to show for it -- aside from 15 bonus checks in 15 UFC appearances -- were two missed opportunities to be an undisputed champion. His fourth-round TKO of Topuria got Gaethje over the hump. It was a resilient performance in a back-and-forth battle that is a prime candidate for fight of the year. More important for Gaethje: At age 37, he is finally sitting at the top of the mountain.

6. Joshua Van

UFC flyweight champion

Record: 18-2

Last: W (UD) vs. Alexandre Pantoja, Sept. 19

Next: Jan. 30 vs. Manel Kape

Van has been champion since December, but until UFC 331, there were doubters. Van had been handed the belt by default, when his challenge for the title was waved off after 26 seconds because Pantoja dislocated his left elbow. Van went on to defend the title against Tatsuro Taira in May, then faced Pantoja in a rematch at UFC 331. Van produced a clear victory -- his eighth win in a row -- to leave no doubt who rules at 125 pounds.

7. Ciryl Gane

UFC heavyweight champion

Previous ranking: Tied for 8th

Record: 15-2, 1 NC

Last: W (UD) vs. Josh Hokit, Nov. 14

Next: TBA

Gane is unique in that he is the first -- and could very well go down as the only -- heavyweight to face the division's four biggest names in Francis Ngannou, Jon Jones, Tom Aspinall and Pereira. None of those four have fought each other, yet all four have have fought the Frenchman. Gane was 0-2 with a no-contest against that group before he knocked out Pereira in the second round of their interim title fight on the White House lawn. Gane was elevated to undisputed champ after Aspinall, still injured, vacated his title, and the new champ made his first defense against Hokit at UFC 334, winning a slugfest.

8. Arman Tsarukyan

UFC lightweight

Previous ranking: 7

Record: 24-3

Last: W (KO1) vs. Mauricio Ruffy, Sept. 19

Next: TBA

Tsarukyan is right back in the place he was in January 2025 -- on the cusp of a title fight. He withdrew from a challenge of Islam Makhachev one day before UFC 311 because of a back injury, and later in the year he was passed over twice when the UFC was booking lightweight title bouts. But by knocking out Ruffy with an elbow in the first round at UFC 331, Tsarukyan put himself back at the front of the line.

9. Merab Dvalishvili

UFC bantamweight

Previous ranking: Tied for 8th

Record: 21-6

Last: L (UD) vs. Petr Yan, Oct. 24

Next: TBA

Dvalishvili was on one of the most impressive runs through the UFC's bantamweight division ever. Not only did he defeat Sean O'Malley for the second time in nine months at UFC 316, but he showcased a new part of his game, finishing O'Malley with a guillotine. Starting in August 2022, Dvalishvili beat José Aldo, Yan, Henry Cejudo, O'Malley (twice), Umar Nurmagomedov and Cory Sandhagen. But at UFC 323, in an attempt to become the first champion in UFC history to successfully defend a title four times in a calendar year, Dvalishvili lost a rematch with Yan. Their third meeting at UFC 333 was the most competitive in their trilogy, but Dvalishvili fell short again.

10. Alex Pereira

UFC heavyweight

Record: 13-4

Last: L (TKO2) vs. Ciryl Gane, June 14

Next: Dec. 12 vs. Sergei Pavlovich

Pereira made a big splash in the MMA after a world championship career in kickboxing. He joined the UFC in 2021 and became a middleweight champion the following year, then moved on to be a two-time light heavyweight titlist before making an unprecedented bid for a belt in a third weight class when he fought Game at UFC Freedom 250 for an interim heavyweight title. Pereira got knocked out in that fight, but now he's back on his feet and in position to reclaim his position when he faces a fellow title contender, Pavlovich, at UFC 335.

Other fighters receiving votes: Alexandre Pantoja and Sean Strickland.

How our panel voted
Brett Okamoto: 1. Islam Makhachev; 2. Petr Yan; 3. Ilia Topuria; 4. Alexander Volkanovski; 5. Joshua Van; 6. Arman Tsarukyan; 7. Merab Dvalishvili; 8. Ciryl Gane; 9. Alex Pereira; 10. Justin Gaethje.

Carlos Contreras Legaspi: 1. Makhachev; 2. Volkanovski; 3. Gaethje; 4. Topuria; 5. Gane; 6. Yan; 7. Van; 8. Pereira; 9. Dvalishvili; 10. Tsarukyan.

Andrew Davis: 1. Makhachev; 2. Volkanovski; 3. Yan; 4. Gaethje; 5. Topuria; 6. Van; 7. Gane; 8. Tsarukyan; 9 Pereira; 10. Sean Strickland.

Dre Waters: 1. Makhachev; 2. Volkanovski; 3. Yan; 4. Gaethje; 5. Topuria; 6. Van; 7. Dvalishvili; 8. Gane; 9. Pereira; 10. Tsarukyan.

Jeff Wagenheim: 1. Makhachev; 2. Yan; 3. Volkanovski; 4. Van; 5. Gaethje; 6. Tsarukyan; 7. Topuria; 8. Gane; 9. Dvalishvili; 10. Alexandre Pantoja.

stories.headline: As Nike replaces Adidas, is UEFA Champions League star ball on its way out?
stories.summary: Nike will replace Adidas as supplier of UEFA Champions League match balls from next season. Will the famous 'star ball' design soon be no more?
stories.body:
Editor's note: This article was first published on Aug. 26, 2026 and has been updated

The UEFA Champions League and UEFA Women's Champions League match balls will boast a brand new look starting next season after UEFA confirmed on Monday that Nike will be taking over from long-standing provider Adidas as the official supplier for the 2027-28 campaign onwards.

Nike will take the reins for the 2027-28 campaign onward after agreeing a deal to supply the official match balls for all three UEFA club competitions from 2027 to 2031 -- the Champions League, the Europa League and the Conference League. According to The Guardian, that deal is worth around $45 million a year, double the value of the final contract with Adidas.

- Man United, Pochettino's to-do list based on what's gone wrong

- Meet Como's Paz, the heir to Messi's Argentina No. 10 shirt

- Champions League talking points: Are Como the real deal?

With Adidas having supplied the official Champions League match ball since 2001, the "star ball" design has become an emblem of the competition. However, the last we see of the iconic pattern might be in the 2026-27 final.

That's because, as things stand, there are no specific details available as to the designs that Nike has in store. In a statement on Monday, UEFA would only say: "Further details on the match ball designs will be revealed in due course." It is also unclear -- and highly unlikely -- that the American sportswear giant will continue with the star theme popularised by Adidas over the past 25 years, as the German powerhouse reportedly hold the rights to the star ball design.

Nike's designs are therefore likely to be fresh and distinct with the intent of drawing a line under Adidas' tenure as UEFA match ball suppliers while also launching their own, modernised visual identity.

Back in August, Adidas unveiled what will be their final iteration of the "star ball," the preliminary eye-catching colourway of which is currently being used throughout the group phase of the 2026-27 Champions League.

The men's version of the 2026-27 Champions League ball is plastered in a neon-spattered livery that, according to Adidas, has been inspired by players creating colourful moments of magic and personal expression while plugging away at training on cold, foggy training pitches during their quest to attain Champions League greatness.

The design for the women's match ball is a little less abstract. The golden-orange pattern takes its inspiration from the aura of the ring of 11 stars that make up the UWCL emblem, with flashes of metallic purple and silver then adding a dash of visual contrast to the mix.

Both balls are based on the template that Adidas have used for their Champions League match balls since the introduction of the "Finale 1" ball for the 2001-02 season. Since then, over 50 iterations of the UCL star ball have been deployed in the competition -- and that's not including the various hi-vis yellow variants that have been used in winter months over the years.

stories.headline: Sources: MLS side FC Cincy nearing deal to acquire NWSL's Racing
stories.summary: The ownership groups of MLS side FC Cincinnati and the NWSL's Racing Louisville FC are nearing an agreement that would relocate the NWSL team to Cincinnati in 2028, multiple sources told ESPN.
stories.body:
The ownership groups of MLS side FC Cincinnati and the NWSL's Racing Louisville FC are nearing an agreement that would relocate the NWSL team to Cincinnati in 2028, multiple sources told ESPN.

Racing Louisville said in a statement on Tuesday that the team is "actively working through a process to sell" the team, although it did not name a prospective buyer. No agreement has been finalized yet, sources said, and it is not immediately clear what a final sale price could be for the NWSL team.

If a deal is reached, Racing Louisville would play the 2027 NWSL season at Lynn Family Stadium in Louisville, Kentucky, before operations moved 100 miles northeast to Cincinnati in 2028. Once there, Racing would play at TQL Stadium, the 26,000-seat downtown home of the MLS side.

ESPN first reported in September that the two sides were engaged in negotiations.

Soccer Holdings and chairman John Neace own Racing Louisville and began seeking investment earlier this year, as ESPN reported in May.

"As the NWSL has grown, so have the financial demands of competing in the league. Additional investment is needed to support the club's long-term future, and we are actively working through a process to sell Racing to a new ownership group," the Louisville-based club said in a statement Tuesday. "Racing was established to bring top-tier women's professional sports to Louisville -- something meaningful our community could rally around. That vision became reality because of the fans, partners and community members who believed in it and continue to support the club. We are deeply grateful for their roles in making Racing what it is today.

"Further updates will be shared as appropriate. In the meantime, our focus is on supporting our players and staff ahead of the 2027 season."

FC Cincinnati also inquired about purchasing Racing Louisville in recent years, ESPN previously reported. On each previous occasion, however, sources cited personal relationships between ownership groups as an obstacle to a potential sale.

An FC Cincinnati spokesperson provided the following statement to ESPN on Tuesday: "We understand and appreciate the excitement and interest around the possibility of bringing an NWSL team to Cincinnati. The passion for soccer in this community is undeniable, and FC Cincinnati remains deeply committed to supporting the continued growth of the women's game. We are hard at work exploring opportunities to expand our involvement in women's soccer, and we are hopeful to have an update in the near future."

Recently, the situation in Louisville has become more urgent. Racing joined the NWSL ahead of the 2021 NWSL season for an expansion fee of around $2 million. Investment in the league by new owners of other clubs has increased exponentially since then. Expansion teams in Atlanta and Columbus will begin playing in the NWSL in 2028 after paying $165 million and $205 million fees, respectively.

Sources told ESPN that throughout the year NWSL commissioner Jessica Berman has been heavily involved in the process of finding a solution in Louisville.

"Their ownership group has made clear that they are prepared to sell," NWSL commissioner Jessica Berman told ESPN in August. "The trajectory of this league has an investment thesis. Our owners, and the future of the league, need to be aligned in that investment thesis.

"They [Louisville] have made clear that they're not prepared to sign up for that. And so, they're raising capital because they want more financial support to be able to invest in the team, which is an indication of their understanding of what's required."

Racing Louisville averaged just under 5,500 fans per game this year, down slightly from 2025. Only the Chicago Stars averaged fewer fans per game.

Sources across the league said to ESPN that Columbus' $205 million price tag paid earlier this year ostensibly sets a floor for any future team, while adding that the NWSL is exercising caution about any potential sale price for a relocation of Racing Louisville to Cincinnati since those cities are only about 100 miles apart.

FC Cincinnati unsuccessfully bid for a 2026 NWSL expansion team with a group that, at the time, included WNBA star Caitlin Clark. Denver was ultimately awarded that team, the NWSL's 14th, for $110 million.

Racing Louisville was recently valued at $127 million and $140 million by Sportico and Forbes, respectively, ranking it as one of the least valuable franchises in the NWSL.

"Relocation should be a last resort," Berman said in March about her philosophy at large. "We view, in our philosophy of what our teams are, is driven by the idea that these are community assets. And what that means is that the community has to believe and it has to be demonstrated over time, that owners and the league will keep these teams in markets even through periods of transition, team sales, or other ups and downs that might be happening with the club, with their on-field performance.

"That does not mean that it's a red line. It means that we will only consider that under appropriate circumstances, and we will be very judicious and exercise high discretion in those circumstances where we feel that it's appropriate."

Versions of relocation have happened in the past in the NWSL. The North Carolina Courage were previously the Western New York Flash until moving in January of 2017. The NWSL also had a franchise leave Kansas City for Salt Lake City, Utah, then return to Kansas City. Both markets now have teams after the Utah Royals were revived in 2024.

stories.headline: Toronto Tempo win 2027 WNBA draft lottery, land No. 1 pick
stories.summary: The Tempo won the WNBA draft lottery Sunday night, earning the No. 1 pick and potentially the chance to draft USC star JuJu Watkins. The Comets will choose second, followed by the Mystics.
stories.body:
The Toronto Tempo will have the No. 1 pick in the 2027 WNBA draft after winning the draft lottery Sunday night.

After completing its inaugural season in 2026, Toronto becomes the first franchise to have the top pick heading into its second season since the Dream in 2009, when Atlanta selected Angel McCoughtry. The Tempo will make their selection April 12.

Lottery odds are based on teams' two-year cumulative records, except for Portland and Toronto, which were expansion teams in 2026. Their odds were solely based on their records from this past season.

The Houston Comets, formerly the Connecticut Sun (22-66), and Toronto (11-33) had the best odds to land the No. 1 pick, each with 329 chances out of 1,000. This marked the first time since 2015 that two teams had the same odds for the first selection.

The Sun, relocating to Texas from Connecticut this offseason, went 1-2 against Toronto in 2026 -- which is the first tiebreaker -- so the franchise couldn't fall past the third pick. Toronto was guaranteed at least the fourth selection.

"I [felt] like something amazing was going to happen," said Tempo forward Aneesah Morrow, the team's lottery representative. "We're here now ... The future is bright. We have great and amazing players, and we have a country on our back. It feels different when you play like that."

Houston will select second in the draft. All of the other selections are in line with what the odds projected heading into Sunday. Washington, which had the next-best odds after acquiring Chicago's first-round pick in the trade that sent Ariel Atkins to the Sky, will pick third.

Seattle will select at No. 4, followed by Portland at No. 5. The Los Angeles Sparks have the sixth and seventh picks -- one that is their own and the other acquired from Phoenix in the Kelsey Plum trade in August.

USC's JuJu Watkins is projected to go No. 1 in ESPN's latest mock draft released Thursday, with Texas' Madison Booker slotted at No. 2.

Notre Dame's Hannah Hidalgo, Virginia's Kymora Johnson, LSU's Mikaylah Williams, Kansas' S'Mya Nichols and Sarah Cisse of France are projected to round out the lottery picks.

The Tempo had a strong start to their season before veteran Brittney Sykes was sidelined indefinitely because of a plantar fascia injury. After she went down, Toronto went 4-21, including a 12-game losing streak. But Sykes and Marina Mabrey combined to form one of the highest-scoring backcourts in the league.

Toronto has some young talent in Morrow, whom the team acquired in a midseason trade, and last year's No. 6 pick Kiki Rice, who was the team's third-leading scorer but missed nearly two months because of a Grade 2 left ankle sprain. The combination of Mabrey, Sykes and Rice gives the Tempo perimeter depth. However, they are somewhat thin in the front court.

"[Toronto] is amazing," Morrow said. "Ever since I walked in the locker room, from the beginning, I was able to see the chemistry ... it's all about building the future of the Toronto franchise."

The WNBA schedule will increase from 44 to 50 games in the 2027 season, making it the longest in league history. The added games were part of the new collective bargaining agreement, which also vastly increased pay, secured a $2.2 billion media deal and slated six expansion teams to join the league between 2024 and 2030.

The 2027 WNBA season is expected to start May 7 and has a latest possible end date of Oct. 24, sources told ESPN's Alexa Philippou last week.

"We're excited about the momentum; it's never been stronger," said Bethany Donaphin, senior vice president and head of WNBA league operations. "We think there's a demand, and we're excited to expand to 50 games."

The rest of the first-round draft order is: No. 8 New York, No. 9 Dallas, No. 10 Indiana, No. 11 Chicago, No. 12 Chicago, No. 13 Dallas, No. 14 Golden State and No. 15 Minnesota.

stories.headline: Kangaroos bounce Kiwis for fourth-straight Rugby League World Cup title
stories.summary: The Kangaroos have won a fourth-straight Rugby League World Cup, toppling New Zealand 32-12 in Brisbane.
stories.body:
The Kangaroos have punished a disappointing New Zealand, with Reece Walsh running riot in a 32-12 World Cup final waltz.

There was an expectation the Kiwis, searching for their second Cup title and first since 2008, would push Australia all the way after a two-point loss in a pulsating tournament opener.

But the visitors struggled from the outset in Brisbane on Sunday night, Jamayne Isaako's kick-off floating long in a sign of things to come.

Walsh dazzled at fullback for the Kangaroos, his pace, vision and wicked footwork too much as he helped lay on two tries and generally wreak havoc around the ruck and close to the line.

Conversely, Walsh's New Zealand opposite Kalyn Ponga -- International Rugby League's Golden Boot winner on Thursday night -- was unable to get into game.

Australian hooker Harry Grant and halves Tom Dearden and Cam Munster completely outplayed their error-riddled opposites, while the Kangaroos' pack muscled up.

Dearden laid on two first-half tries for Liam Martin with well-timed short balls, while Bradman Best was rewarded for an inspired chase-down tackle of Jahrome Hughes with a try soon after.

When Tom Trbojevic scored to begin the second half it was 28-6 and effectively game over.

Jack Bostock completed his breakout season with a try in each half for Australia.

It was the Kangaroos' fourth consecutive title and 10th in the last 11 tournaments, dating back to 1975.

stories.headline: Lando Norris, Max Verstappen confident in F1's decision to race in Middle East
stories.summary: Lando Norris is confident Formula 1 bosses are not putting the sport's 2,000-strong travelling circus at risk by ending the season in the Middle East.
stories.body:
Lando Norris is confident Formula 1 bosses are not putting the sport's 2,000-strong travelling circus at risk by ending the season in the Middle East.

Following Saturday's race on the Las Vegas Strip, the grid's 11 teams -- 10 of which have bases in the UK -- will head to Qatar for the penultimate round on Nov. 29 before a concluding fixture in Abu Dhabi the following weekend.

Imola had been placed on standby to host the final race amid the ongoing United States-Iran conflict.

However, F1 chiefs confirmed last week that they will push ahead with completing the 23-round season, as planned, in the Middle East.

UK's current Foreign Office advice says the situation in the region "remains deeply unpredictable and the risk of escalation is high."

It adds that "British nationals in, or planning to travel through, the Middle East should be prepared for possible flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions," as well as "a risk of further attacks across the region at short notice."

But speaking in Las Vegas, 27-year-old Norris, who won the previous race in São Paulo, said: "I am looking forward to going. From my side, I am fine. It is a big team that we travel with, and it is more, 'what do they think?'

"But I have my friend's wedding in Bahrain next week, so I was planning on going there anyway, and then going on to Qatar and Abu Dhabi.

"So, from my side, it is not a concern. I just don't believe that this sport would put us at risk."

The rounds in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia were cancelled earlier this year, although a 'Bahrain Grand Prix' was relocated to Malaysia's Sepang venue last month. Next year's calendar is due to begin in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia.

- The rebuild and redemption of Liam Lawson, F1's comeback kid

- Max Verstappen: I don't need Kimi Antonelli to motivate me to stay in F1

- Las Vegas Grand Prix 2026: Race start time, how to watch, full schedule, predictions

"I don't have any hesitation to go or know of anyone that is concerned," said Mercedes driver George Russell ahead of the concluding two rounds.

"I am sure some people have their reservations. But I know people who live in the region, and they have said it quite bluntly, that if they didn't feel comfortable, they wouldn't remain there with their families.

"There are a lot of terrible things going on in every region of the world, and you have got to trust in the people that say it is safe. F1 are not stupid, so there is zero concern from my side. Fingers crossed it'll all be fine."

Max Verstappen, who previously said in September that he would prefer F1 not to race in the Middle East, said otherwise in Vegas.

Verstappen, quoted by BBC Sport, said: "I trust F1 and FIA to make the right call on that, right?

"I don't have all the intel. I'm not an officer. I just hope that they make the right call on that. And that's all that you can rely on, really.

"They also send over their findings and understanding. So I trust them."

Kimi Antonelli was crowned world champion last month in Mexico, while his Mercedes team wrapped up the constructors' title the following weekend in São Paulo.

Red Bull's Verstappen leads the battle to finish as runner-up in the drivers' standings. The four-time world champion is 17 points clear of Russell and 18 ahead of Lewis Hamilton ahead of Saturday's night race.
